Neonatal Blacktip sawtail catsharks emerge from their egg cases at a remarkably modest size, with field measurements confirming a total length at birth of 6 cm [Lb = 6 cm]. This diminutive starting point places newborn pups among the smallest elasmobranch neonates relative to adult dimensions, and the yolk-dependent embryos within the mermaid's purses undergo substantial organogenesis before hatching. During this early exotrophic transition, the young individuals rely entirely on their endogenous reserves until the yolk-sac resorption is complete, at which point active feeding onset commences. The relatively small birth size likely reflects an energetic trade-off between producing larger, more developed offspring and maintaining the fecundity necessary for population persistence in the deep waters this species inhabits. Comparative studies among congeners suggest that this neonatal size is consistent with an overall life-history strategy characterized by moderate growth rates and delayed maturation, both of which are common in demersal sharks inhabiting continental slopes. The selection pressures favoring small size at independence may be linked to the abundance of small benthic invertebrates that constitute the primary prey for newly foraging pups.

As individuals progress through the juvenile and sub-adult stages, they experience sustained somatic growth that ultimately culminates in the attainment of their maximum recorded body dimensions. Comprehensive field surveys and captive observations indicate that the ultimate total length for this species reaches 46 cm [Li = 46 cm], although some regional variation has been documented. Interestingly, a second, slightly smaller asymptotic value of 42 cm [Li = 42 cm] has also been reported from other study populations, suggesting that local environmental conditions or resource availability may modulate the final size these sharks achieve as sexually mature adults. The discrepancy between these two reported asymptotes likely reflects differences in sampling methodology or geographic variation across the species' range within the western Pacific. Growing juveniles typically add several centimeters per year during their early life, with growth rates decelerating markedly once individuals approach the ultimate length. This asymptotic growth pattern is characteristic of many elasmobranchs and stands in contrast to the indeterminate growth observed in some teleost fishes. The larger asymptotic length of 46 cm [Li = 46 cm] appears to be more representative of individuals inhabiting deeper, cooler waters where metabolic demands are lower and resource partitioning may be more favorable for sustained growth.

Puberty in the Blacktip sawtail catshark occurs at a total length that differs between the sexes, reflecting the distinct energetic constraints associated with gamete production. For females, the total length at puberty is 40.5 cm [Lp = 40.5 cm], a size at which ovarian maturation begins and the first viable oocytes are produced. In males, testicular recrudescence and the onset of spermatogenesis become apparent at a somewhat smaller body size, with the total length at puberty for males recorded at 34.5 cm [Lp = 34.5 cm]. This sexual dimorphism in maturation size is a widespread pattern among elasmobranchs and is typically attributed to the greater somatic investment females must make to support developing embryos and produce large, yolk-rich eggs. The onset of gonad maturation does not coincide immediately with first reproduction, as a period of physiological adjustment follows puberty during which individuals accumulate the necessary energy reserves for successful breeding. The attainment of these pubertal lengths represents a critical life-history transition, marking the shift from purely somatic growth to the dual demands of body maintenance and reproductive allocation. Juveniles below these thresholds are considered immature individuals incapable of contributing to the next generation.

Reproductive output in Galeus sauteri is modest, with females producing approximately 2 eggs per season [Ri = approximately 2 eggs per season] when maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This corresponds to roughly 2 eggs per year [Ri = roughly 2 eggs per year], reflecting a relatively low maximum reproductive rate that is typical of many deep-sea sharks with slow life histories. The single annual reproductive event yields a pair of encapsulated embryos that develop slowly within their leathery egg cases before hatching. This limited fecundity, combined with the late age at maturity implied by the substantial pubertal lengths, makes the species inherently vulnerable to overexploitation and population decline. The reproductive strategy of producing a small number of well-provisioned offspring is consistent with the broader K-selected life-history syndrome observed in most elasmobranchs, particularly those inhabiting stable but resource-limited environments. Field studies suggest that not all mature females reproduce every year, further reducing the effective population fecundity. The temperature at which these reproductive measurements were taken is critical, as metabolic rates and thus the timing of reproductive events are heavily influenced by ambient thermal conditions experienced by gravid female sharks.

Longevity estimates for the Blacktip sawtail catshark, derived from captive maintenance studies conducted at a constant water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years]. This extended lifespan is characteristic of many deep-water elasmobranchs and reflects the slow-paced life history that accompanies their modest growth rates and low reproductive output. The combination of a 20-year (20 years) [am = 20 years] lifespan with a late onset of puberty and minimal annual fecundity creates a demographic profile in which population turnover is exceptionally slow at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Natural mortality rates among adults are presumably low, as senescence and age-related death typically occur only after several decades in such long-lived species. Age validation through vertebral banding patterns has corroborated these captive longevity records, confirming that individuals regularly persist for two decades under favorable conditions. The thermal regime at which these estimates were obtained is representative of the species' natural deep-sea habitat, where temperatures remain consistently cool throughout the year. This remarkable longevity, when coupled with the species' modest size at birth (6 cm) [Lb = 6 cm] and the 46 cm [Li = 46 cm] asymptotic length, underscores the extreme contrast between early-life vulnerability and prolonged adult persistence that defines the life history of the Blacktip sawtail catshark.
